solution:
Bohr made three postulates.

**1. The electrons revolve around the nucleus in circular orbits.** This is the same assumption as in Rutherford's model: the centripetal force necessary for the circular motion is provided by the electrostatic force of attraction between the electron and the nucleus.

**2. The radius of the orbit of an electron can only take certain fixed values, such that the angular momentum of the electron in these orbits is an integral multiple of \(h/2\pi\)**, \(h\) being Planck's constant. That is, \(m_e \mathrm{v}_n r_n = n\dfrac{h}{2\pi}\), \(n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots\). Such orbits are called stable orbits, and an electron in such an orbit does not emit radiation even though classical physics demands that it should.

**3. An electron can make a transition from one of its orbits to another orbit having lower energy. In doing so it emits a photon of energy equal to the difference in its energies in the two orbits**, i.e. \(h\nu = E_m - E_n\).

Rutherford's model faced the following difficulties.

**1. It could not account for the stability of the atom.** By Maxwell's electromagnetic theory an accelerated charge radiates energy. An electron moving in a circular orbit is continuously accelerated (its speed is constant but its direction changes all the time), so it should radiate continuously. Losing energy, the radius of its orbit would shrink continuously and it would spiral into the nucleus, so the atom would collapse. In fact atoms are stable.

**2. It could not explain the observed line spectra.** As the electron spiralled inwards its speed, and hence the frequency of the radiation emitted, would change continuously, so every atom should give a continuous spectrum. What is actually observed is that atoms emit radiation only of certain definite frequencies, giving a line spectrum.

**3. Atoms do not radiate on their own.** They have to be supplied energy, for example by heating, before they emit at all.

Rutherford's model failed on all these counts.

**Alpha decay:** the parent nucleus emits an alpha particle, which is the nucleus of a helium atom, so it loses two protons and two neutrons:

\(^{A}_{Z}\text{X} \rightarrow {}^{A-4}_{Z-2}\text{Y} + \alpha\)

It occurs in heavy nuclei, in which the electrostatic repulsion between the large number of protons cannot be contained by the attractive nuclear force.

**Beta decay:** the nucleus emits an electron produced by converting a neutron into a proton, \(n \rightarrow p + e^{-} +\) antineutrino, so the mass number is unchanged while \(Z\) increases by one:

\(^{A}_{Z}\text{X} \rightarrow {}^{A}_{Z+1}\text{Y} + e^{-} +\) antineutrino

There is also **beta plus decay**, in which a proton inside the nucleus is converted to a neutron with the emission of a positron, so that \(Z\) decreases by one:

\(^{A}_{Z}\text{X} \rightarrow {}^{A}_{Z-1}\text{Y} + e^{+} +\) neutrino

**Gamma decay:** a nucleus left in an excited state after an alpha or beta decay makes a transition to a lower nuclear energy level and emits the excess energy as a high energy photon, a gamma ray. Neither \(A\) nor \(Z\) changes; the daughter nucleus is the same nucleus with less energy.

**Excitation energy** of an electron in the \(n^{\text{th}}\) orbit is the difference between its energy in that orbit and its energy in the ground state, i.e. the energy that must be supplied to raise the electron from the ground state to that excited state. For hydrogen the minimum excitation energy (to \(n = 2\)) is \(-3.4 - (-13.6) = 10.2\ \text{eV}\).

**Ionization energy** of an atom is the minimum amount of energy that must be given to an electron in the ground state of that atom to set the electron free, i.e. to raise its total energy to zero. For hydrogen it is \(13.6\ \text{eV}\).

**Binding energy** of the electron is the energy with which the electron is bound to the nucleus — the same amount of energy that would be released if the atom were formed by bringing the electron and the nucleus together from infinity. For an electron in the ground state of hydrogen it is \(13.6\ \text{eV}\), numerically equal to the ionization energy.

For hydrogen \((Z = 1)\) Rydberg's formula gives the frequency of a line as

\(\nu = \dfrac{c}{\lambda} = cR_H\left(\dfrac{1}{n^2} - \dfrac{1}{m^2}\right)\)

**First line of the Lyman series** \((n = 1, m = 2)\):

\(\nu_1 = cR_H\left(\dfrac{1}{1^2} - \dfrac{1}{2^2}\right) = \dfrac{3}{4}cR_H\)

**Limiting frequency of the Lyman series** — the series limit is reached as \(m \rightarrow \infty\) with \(n = 1\):

\(\nu_{L} = cR_H\left(\dfrac{1}{1^2} - 0\right) = cR_H\)

**Limiting frequency of the Balmer series** \((n = 2,\ m \rightarrow \infty)\):

\(\nu_{B} = cR_H\left(\dfrac{1}{2^2} - 0\right) = \dfrac{cR_H}{4}\)

Therefore the difference between the two limiting frequencies is

\(\nu_{L} - \nu_{B} = cR_H - \dfrac{cR_H}{4} = \dfrac{3}{4}cR_H = \nu_1\)

which is exactly the frequency of the first line of the Lyman series. Hence proved.

[Textbook misprint: the book prints Eq. (15.7) as \(E_n = -m_e Z^2 e^4 / (8\varepsilon_0 h^2 n^2)\), with \(\varepsilon_0\) to the first power. It must be \(\varepsilon_0^{2}\), as the derivation above shows and as a dimensional check confirms; with a single \(\varepsilon_0\) the expression does not even have the dimensions of energy. The same dropped square appears in the book's expression for \(h\nu\) and in Eqs. (15.9) and (15.10) on the next page, so it is one typesetting slip repeated four times.]

**The postulates**

1. The electrons revolve around the nucleus in circular orbits, the necessary centripetal force being the electrostatic attraction of the nucleus.
2. Only those orbits are allowed for which the angular momentum of the electron is an integral multiple of \(h/2\pi\); these are stable orbits and an electron in one of them does not radiate.
3. When an electron makes a transition to an orbit of lower energy it emits a photon whose energy equals the difference of the two orbital energies.

**Derivation of the energy of the electron**

Let the electron of mass \(m_e\) move with speed \(\mathrm{v}_n\) in the \(n^{\text{th}}\) orbit of radius \(r_n\) about a nucleus of atomic number \(Z\). From the second postulate,

\(m_e \mathrm{v}_n r_n = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}\)  ... (1)

The electrostatic attraction supplies the centripetal force, so

\(\dfrac{m_e \mathrm{v}_n^{2}}{r_n} = \dfrac{Ze^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r_n^{2}}\)  ... (2)

Eliminating \(\mathrm{v}_n\) between (1) and (2),

\(r_n = \dfrac{n^{2}h^{2}\varepsilon_0}{\pi m_e Z e^{2}}\)  ... (3)

The total energy is the sum of the kinetic and the electrostatic potential energy. From (2), \(m_e\mathrm{v}_n^{2} = \dfrac{Ze^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r_n}\), so

\(\text{K.E.} = \dfrac{1}{2}m_e\mathrm{v}_n^{2} = \dfrac{Ze^{2}}{8\pi\varepsilon_0 r_n}\), and \(\text{P.E.} = -\dfrac{Ze^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r_n}\)

\(\therefore E_n = \dfrac{Ze^{2}}{8\pi\varepsilon_0 r_n} - \dfrac{Ze^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r_n} = -\dfrac{Ze^{2}}{8\pi\varepsilon_0 r_n}\)

Substituting \(r_n\) from (3),

\(E_n = -\dfrac{m_e Z^{2} e^{4}}{8\varepsilon_0^{2} h^{2} n^{2}}\)

The negative sign shows the electron is bound to the nucleus. For hydrogen \((Z = 1)\), substituting the values of the constants,

\(E_n = -\dfrac{13.6}{n^{2}}\ \text{eV}\)

The energy of the electron in the \(n^{\text{th}}\) orbit is

\(E_n = -\dfrac{m_e Z^{2} e^{4}}{8\varepsilon_0^{2} h^{2} n^{2}}\)

When the electron makes a transition from the \(m^{\text{th}}\) to the \(n^{\text{th}}\) orbit \((m > n)\) the excess energy is emitted as a photon of frequency \(\nu\):

\(h\nu = E_m - E_n = \dfrac{m_e Z^{2} e^{4}}{8\varepsilon_0^{2} h^{2}}\left(\dfrac{1}{n^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{m^{2}}\right)\)

Writing \(\nu = c/\lambda\),

\(\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = \dfrac{m_e Z^{2} e^{4}}{8c\,\varepsilon_0^{2} h^{3}}\left(\dfrac{1}{n^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{m^{2}}\right) = R_H Z^{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{n^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{m^{2}}\right)\)

where \(R_H = \dfrac{m_e e^{4}}{8c\,\varepsilon_0^{2} h^{3}} = 1.097 \times 10^{7}\ \text{m}^{-1}\) is Rydberg's constant. For hydrogen \(Z = 1\).

**Lyman series** \((n = 1,\ m = 2, 3, 4, \ldots)\):

\(\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R_H\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{m^{2}}\right)\)

**Balmer series** \((n = 2,\ m = 3, 4, 5, \ldots)\):

\(\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R_H\left(\dfrac{1}{4} - \dfrac{1}{m^{2}}\right)\)

**Shortest wavelengths.** The shortest wavelength in a series is its series limit, obtained by letting \(m \rightarrow \infty\), which gives \(\lambda_{\min} = n^{2}/R_H\).

Lyman: \(\lambda_{\min} = \dfrac{1}{R_H} = \dfrac{1}{1.097 \times 10^{7}} = 9.116 \times 10^{-8}\ \text{m} = 911.6\) Å

Balmer: \(\lambda_{\min} = \dfrac{4}{R_H} = 3.646 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m} = 3646\) Å

The angular speed of the electron in the \(n^{\text{th}}\) orbit is \(\omega_n = \dfrac{\mathrm{v}_n}{r_n}\).

For hydrogen \((Z = 1)\), \(\mathrm{v}_n = \dfrac{e^{2}}{2\varepsilon_0 h n}\) and \(r_n = \dfrac{n^{2}h^{2}\varepsilon_0}{\pi m_e e^{2}}\), so

\(\omega_n = \dfrac{e^{2}}{2\varepsilon_0 h n} \times \dfrac{\pi m_e e^{2}}{n^{2}h^{2}\varepsilon_0} = \dfrac{\pi m_e e^{4}}{2\varepsilon_0^{2} h^{3} n^{3}}\)

Since \(\mathrm{v}_n \propto 1/n\) and \(r_n \propto n^{2}\), the angular speed varies as \(1/n^{3}\). It is therefore **maximum for the smallest orbit, the ground state \(n = 1\)**:

\(\omega_{\max} = \dfrac{\pi m_e e^{4}}{2\varepsilon_0^{2} h^{3}}\)

\(= \dfrac{\pi \times 9.109 \times 10^{-31} \times (1.602 \times 10^{-19})^{4}}{2 \times (8.854 \times 10^{-12})^{2} \times (6.626 \times 10^{-34})^{3}}\)

\(= 4.13 \times 10^{16}\ \text{rad s}^{-1}\)

(As a check, \(\mathrm{v}_1 = 2.187 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m s}^{-1}\) and \(r_1 = 5.29 \times 10^{-11}\ \text{m}\), giving \(\omega_1 = \mathrm{v}_1/r_1 = 4.13 \times 10^{16}\ \text{rad s}^{-1}\).)

**Alpha decay.** The parent nucleus emits an alpha particle (a helium nucleus), losing two protons and two neutrons:

\(^{A}_{Z}\text{X} \rightarrow {}^{A-4}_{Z-2}\text{Y} + \alpha\)

Heavy nuclei decay this way because the electrostatic repulsion among their many protons is no longer contained by the attractive nuclear force. The energy released, which appears as the kinetic energy of the products, is

\(Q = \left[m_X - m_Y - m_{He}\right]c^{2}\)

where the masses are the ATOMIC masses of the parent, the daughter and helium (the electron counts then balance on the two sides).

**Beta decay.** In beta minus decay a neutron in the nucleus becomes a proton, \(n \rightarrow p + e^{-} +\) antineutrino, so

\(^{A}_{Z}\text{X} \rightarrow {}^{A}_{Z+1}\text{Y} + e^{-} +\) antineutrino

In beta plus decay a proton becomes a neutron, \(p \rightarrow n + e^{+} +\) neutrino, so

\(^{A}_{Z}\text{X} \rightarrow {}^{A}_{Z-1}\text{Y} + e^{+} +\) neutrino

In terms of NUCLEAR masses the energy released in either case is

\(Q = \left[m_X - m_Y - m_e\right]c^{2}\)

If ATOMIC masses are used instead, the electrons must be counted: the daughter atom of a beta minus decay already carries the extra electron, so \(Q = [m_X - m_Y]c^{2}\), while for beta plus decay \(Q = [m_X - m_Y - 2m_e]c^{2}\).

**Gamma decay.** A nucleus left in an excited state after an alpha or a beta decay drops to a lower nuclear energy level and emits the excess energy as a high energy photon:

\(^{A}_{Z}\text{X}^{*} \rightarrow {}^{A}_{Z}\text{X} + \gamma\)

Neither \(A\) nor \(Z\) changes. The energy of the gamma ray is the difference between the two nuclear energy levels,

\(E_{\gamma} = h\nu = E_{\text{excited}} - E_{\text{lower}}\)

**Nuclear fission** is the process in which a heavy nucleus breaks into two lighter nuclei with the release of energy. The binding energy per nucleon \(E_B/A\) is largest for middle-weight nuclei \((A \approx 50\ \text{to}\ 80)\) and smaller for very heavy nuclei, so when a heavy nucleus splits, the products are more tightly bound, their combined mass is less than that of the parent, and the difference appears as energy.

Example: \(^{236}_{92}\text{U} \rightarrow {}^{140}_{56}\text{Ba} + {}^{94}_{36}\text{Kr} + 2n\)

The energy generated is

\(Q = \left[m_U - m_{Ba} - m_{Kr} - 2m_n\right]c^{2}\)

or in general \(Q = \left[m_{\text{parent}} - \sum m_{\text{products}}\right]c^{2}\).

**Nuclear fusion** is the process in which two light nuclei come together to form a heavier nucleus, again with a release of energy. Light nuclei \((A < 40)\) have a smaller \(E_B/A\) than the heavier nucleus they form, so the product is more tightly bound and energy of the order of MeV is released. The nuclei must approach within about 1 fm for the nuclear force to act, which requires very high temperatures to overcome their electrostatic repulsion.

Example, the reaction inside the Sun: \(4p \rightarrow \alpha + 2e^{+} +\) neutrinos

The energy generated is

\(Q = \left[4m_p - m_{\alpha} - 2m_e\right]c^{2}\)

or in general \(Q = \left[\sum m_{\text{reactants}} - m_{\text{product}}\right]c^{2}\).

**Principles of a nuclear reactor.** A nuclear reactor is a device in which nuclear fission is carried out in a controlled manner so that the energy released can be collected as heat and converted into electricity.

1. **Fuel.** \(^{235}_{92}\text{U}\) is used as the fuel. It absorbs a slow neutron to become \(^{236}_{92}\text{U}\), which then undergoes fission, \(^{235}_{92}\text{U} + n \rightarrow {}^{236}_{92}\text{U}\).

2. **Chain reaction.** Each fission releases on average about 2.7 neutrons. These are absorbed by other \(^{235}_{92}\text{U}\) nuclei, which fission in turn, so the number of fissions can grow rapidly. This cascade is called a chain reaction.

3. **Slowing the neutrons.** Fission of \(^{235}\text{U}\) is caused by slow neutrons, so the fast neutrons produced have to be slowed down.

4. **Control.** The reactor must not be allowed to run away. Methods are employed to absorb the surplus neutrons so that on average only one neutron from each fission goes on to cause a further fission. The rate of fission, and so the rate of energy generation, is then steady.

5. **Heat removal.** The energy appears as the kinetic energy of the fission products, i.e. as heat. It is carried away and used to raise steam, which drives turbines to generate electricity.

**Difference between a nuclear reactor and a nuclear bomb.** In both, energy comes from the fission chain reaction. In a **reactor** the chain reaction is CONTROLLED — the neutron population is held steady so that energy is released slowly and continuously at a useful rate, and the heat is carried away and converted to electricity. In a **nuclear bomb** the chain reaction is UNCONTROLLED — the number of fissions multiplies without check, so an extremely large amount of energy is released in a very short time, producing an explosion.

[Textbook misprint: part (a) is printed as \(^{226}_{86}\text{Ra}\). Radium has atomic number 88, not 86 (86 is radon); the book itself writes \(^{223}_{88}\text{Ra}\) in the very next question. The decay has been completed above for radium, \(Z = 88\).]

In every nuclear decay the mass number \(A\) and the charge number \(Z\) are separately conserved, and that fixes the missing particle.

**(a)** An alpha particle is \(^{4}_{2}\text{He}\), so the daughter has \(A = 226 - 4 = 222\) and \(Z = 88 - 2 = 86\), which is radon:

\(^{226}_{88}\text{Ra} \rightarrow \alpha + {}^{222}_{86}\text{Rn}\)

(Radium has \(Z = 88\); the subscript 86 printed against Ra in the question is a misprint, and the book itself writes \(^{223}_{88}\text{Ra}\) in the next question.)

**(b)** This is a beta minus decay: \(A\) is unchanged and \(Z\) increases by one, giving fluorine, and an antineutrino is emitted with the electron:

\(^{19}_{8}\text{O} \rightarrow e^{-} + {}^{19}_{9}\text{F} +\) antineutrino

**(c)** Again an alpha particle is emitted, so \(A = 228 - 4 = 224\) and \(Z = 90 - 2 = 88\), which is radium:

\(^{228}_{90}\text{Th} \rightarrow \alpha + {}^{224}_{88}\text{Ra}\)

**(d)** Here \(A\) is unchanged while \(Z\) falls from 7 to 6, so a proton has become a neutron. This is a beta plus decay, in which a positron and a neutrino are emitted:

\(^{12}_{7}\text{N} \rightarrow {}^{12}_{6}\text{C} + e^{+} +\) neutrino
